verdict: Last Circle's *informational* feedback layer is genuinely commercial-grade — coalesced colour-coded damage numbers, a priority-queued announcement system, spatialised limited audio, directional threat indicators and a death recap that beats most AAA death screens — but its *physical* feedback layer is close to absent: pulling the trigger produces no camera kick, no view-model movement, no FOV punch and no hitstop, and camShake is written in exactly two places in the entire codebase (explosions and taking damage), neither of which is your own gun. The result is a game that tells you what happened with excellent clarity but never makes you *feel* it, which is precisely the axis that separates a hobby build from a commercial product.
what_last_circle_does: FX (runtime/3d/royale/fx.js, 255 lines): ONE InstancedMesh pool of 1024 unlit cubes, single draw call, ring-buffer allocated. Nine event listeners: shotFired, tracer, impact, explosion, swimState, swimStroke, actorHurt, actorDied, chestOpened. Muzzle flash = 6 cubes, size 0.17, life 0.10s, drag 5, spawned at the right-hand bone matrixWorld plus a per-weapon barrel length (pistol 0.5m → sniper 1.15m), NOT at the eye. Tracers = one stretched instance per projectile, per-weapon colour (sniper 0x9fe0ff, glauncher 0xffb060, shotgun 0xffc46a, default 0xffd24a), length 7/4/3 units, life 0.22s, with a deliberate cosmetic speed cap of 200 m/s so 999 m/s hitscan rounds are actually visible. Impact = 5 cubes, colour by surface (flesh 0xc23b3b, build 0xd7c08a, stone 0xa9a9a9, dirt 0x9a7f4f). Explosion = 26 fire cubes (speed 11, up 5, size 0.28, life 0.8) + 14 smoke cubes (size 0.4, life 1.4, gravity -1.5). Death = 12 white/blue cubes. Damage numbers are DOM elements projected from world space, 26px 900-weight, life 1.05s, rising 0.9 u/s, colour gold #ffd54a headshot > blue #6db9ff shield > white #ffffff body, coalesced per victim per frame so a 9-pellet shotgun blast prints one "117" instead of nine "13"s. CAMERA SHAKE: `grep -rn "camShake *=" runtime/` returns exactly 4 lines — init to 0, explosion `(1 - d/40) * 0.5` within 40m, `0.12` when the player is hurt, and decay `dt * 1.8`. Consumed in player.js:1079-1081 as pure per-frame white noise on cam.position.x (full amplitude) and .y (0.6x) — translational only, no rotational roll, no smooth-noise curve. Firing your own weapon sets camShake nowhere. Recoil (weapons.js:432) is aim-pitch only: pistol 0.008 rad (0.46°), smg 0.006 (0.34°), ar 0.011 (0.63°), shotgun 0.03 (1.72°), sniper 0.05 (2.86°), glauncher 0.035 (2.01°), recovered at 0.12 rad/s — at the AR's 330 rpm (0.18s interval) 0.0216 rad recovers against an 0.011 rad kick, so recoil fully re-centres between every shot and no weapon ever builds a climbing pattern. FOV (player.js:1090) reacts only to ADS/scope/sprint, never to firing. `a.weaponMesh` is a static clone parented to the hand bone — no fire kick, no reload animation, no equip animation. Hitmarker: ✕ glyph, 26px white / 34px gold on headshot, 120ms / 170ms, with head-priority latching so a body pellet can't overwrite a head pellet inside one blast; audio ping 950 Hz body / 1400 Hz head; kill confirm is a 700→1050 Hz two-tone but the ✕ itself never changes on a kill. Hurt tint (hud.js:1261, 1429) is a red radial vignette at 0.4 alpha shown for a flat 0.7s after ANY damage — binary, not scaled by damage taken or by remaining HP. Audio (audio.js): fully procedural Web Audio, per-class noise burst + tuned lowpass (pistol 1400 Hz/0.09s/0.32 gain … sniper 500 Hz/0.32s/0.66 gain) with a square-wave crack layer on AR and sniper, gains deliberately trimmed ~35% at owner request; spatial pan projected onto the corrected camera-right vector, gunshots audible to 260m; a brickwall DynamicsCompressor at -6 dBFS / 20:1 / 3ms attack on the master bus so a 9-pellet blast plus an explosion cannot clip. Reload is a 4-beat mechanical sequence timed to reloadS (mag click 0ms → mag drop 110ms → mag seat 55% → slide rack 86%), not a beep. Victory: `endMatch` holds the live 3D world for 2600ms (skippable on any key/click) while a 34px Orbitron "VICTORY ROYALE" banner shows, plus a 4-note triangle sting (523/659/784/1046 Hz) and an endgame music track; then a DOM panel with 60 CSS-transition confetti divs. Kill streaks escalate DOUBLE → TRIPLE → QUAD → RAMPAGE. Bloom is on but turned down to strength 0.14 in-match (maps.js:282). NO hitstop, NO decals, NO shell casings, NO dynamic lights for muzzle or explosion, NO enemy hit-flash, NO ragdoll (death anim then silent removal at 4500ms), NO fx listener for propBreak / hardLand / landed / levelUp / pickedUp.
what_benchmarks_do: FINAL DROP (crazygames.com/game/final-drop): verified 9.2/10 rating over the last 6 months, released June 2026, last updated 17 June 2026, browser desktop-only, 100 players, building (walls/floors/ramps), destructible trees/rocks/structures as the resource loop, Shift as a run/walk TOGGLE, B/N emotes, mode menu. Its hit-feedback layer is NOT documented anywhere I could reach — the CrazyGames, final-drop.com and Miniplay pages carry marketing copy only, and no review or teardown surfaced. Every claim I make about Final Drop's juice specifically is therefore UNVERIFIED and I am not asserting any. What I can assert: a 9.2-rated commercial browser BR whose core loop is "destroy trees, rocks and structures for materials" necessarily ships destruction VFX on every structure break, because that action happens dozens of times per match. FORTNITE (verified via search): headshot damage numbers are yellow rather than white, with a distinct audio cue on the hit; damage-number style is a player setting (Cumulative vs List); Reticle Damage Feedback is a setting (Hit & Icons / Hit Only / Off); the headshot hitmarker sound was changed in Chapter 7 and after backlash Epic shipped a Default/Legacy toggle in Audio settings — i.e. the hitmarker sound is a first-class, individually-tuned, player-configurable asset. APEX LEGENDS (verified): damage numbers encode the target's armour state — white/blue/purple shield tiers, red when you are into health, gold on a headshot — so the number is a tactical read, not just a hit confirm. VLAMBEER, "The Art of Screenshake" (Jan Willem Nijman, INDIGO 2013 — the canonical game-feel reference, verified): the named techniques include gun kickback, sleep/hitstop (pausing for a frame or a few when enemies die, the player is hit, or things explode), permanence (shells on the ground, smoke from explosions, corpses that persist so the world remembers the fight), bigger bullets, muzzle flash, and a camera that moves with the player. Last Circle ships muzzle flash and bigger/visible bullets; it ships none of kickback, sleep, or permanence. Scaled honestly to browser WebGL: hitstop, camera kick, view-model recoil, additive flash sprites, pooled decal quads and shell casings are all cheap — they are frame-budget-free or near-free and are what browser games actually use instead of the AAA route of ragdolls, dynamic lights and animated first-person arms.
strengths: Damage-number semantics match the AAA convention and the coalescing is better than most: gold headshot / blue shield / white body (fx.js:198-199) is the Fortnite-yellow-headshot plus Apex-shield-colour read, and the per-frame hurtBuf Map means a 9-pellet shotgun blast prints one readable '117' rather than nine stacked '13's. Fortnite ships this as a user setting called Cumulative; Last Circle just does the right thing by default.

The tracer decision is the sharpest single piece of feel engineering in the file. Hitscan weapons run at speed: 999 in the sim, which crosses the screen inside one frame and is invisible; fx.js:108 caps the COSMETIC bolt at 200 m/s while the damage ray has already resolved. That is exactly the trick commercial shooters use, arrived at deliberately, with per-weapon colour and length (sniper 7 units and 0x9fe0ff, shotgun 4 units, launcher 3 units).

Muzzle flash erupts from the actual barrel, not the camera: weapons.js:444-450 reads the right-hand bone's matrixWorld and pushes forward by a per-weapon barrel length (pistol 0.5m, ar 0.95m, sniper 1.15m). In a third-person-default game (camera dist 4.2m) this is what stops the 'firing from the face' look, and most hobby builds never fix it.

Audio engineering is the standout. Procedural per-class synthesis with distinct filter curves (sniper 500Hz/0.32s vs smg 1800Hz/0.06s), a square-wave crack layer on rifles only, correctly-derived stereo pan (the comment at audio.js:104-109 documents finding and fixing a sign error that put every positional sound in the wrong ear), 260m gunshot range, and a -6 dBFS / 20:1 / 3ms brickwall limiter on the master so 9 pellets plus an explosion cannot clip the hardware. Browser games essentially never ship a limiter.

Reload is a four-beat mechanical sequence timed to the weapon's real reloadS — mag release click, mag drop at 110ms, mag seat at 55%, slide rack at 86% (audio.js:232-240). That is the sound-design equivalent of a reload animation, and it partly compensates for having no reload animation at all.

The announcement priority queue (hud.js:1918-1949) solves a problem AAA games routinely get wrong: victory 3 > elimination/level-up 2 > milestone/deploy 1, with equal-or-lower priority QUEUEING rather than being dropped. The inline comment documents the exact failure it fixes — the 'ELIMINATED X' banner for the kill that took the lobby to 10 being overwritten by '10 REMAIN' before the browser ever painted it. That is the kill you most want to see, and it is now protected.
Kill-streak escalation is present and correctly tiered: DOUBLE / TRIPLE / QUAD / RAMPAGE at 2/3/4/5+ (hud.js:1850).

Directional threat feedback is genuinely Apex/PUBG-tier: gold chevrons for gunfire between 12m and 250m, red arcs for damage taken pointed at the attacker, and greyscale footstep glyphs scanned at 3Hz for actors moving faster than 2 m/s within 30m, all positioned on a screen-centred ring at 0.36 * min(viewport) with per-kind lifetimes (damage 1.6s, shot 1.2s, footstep 0.9s).

The death recap (hud.js:2000-2027) is better than Fortnite's or Apex's on the one question that actually matters emotionally: it prints FINAL BLOW distance and HEADSHOT, YOU DEALT n damage, THEY HAD LEFT n HP, and literally prints 'SO CLOSE.' when the killer survived under 25 HP. That is a real emotional beat, correctly identified and correctly executed.

The 2600ms hold on the live 3D world after the winning kill before cutting to the stats panel (ffg_royale3d.js:319-336), skippable on any input, is the right call and the comment shows it was a deliberate fix for the banner being destroyed in the frame it was born.

Architecture is correct for the medium: one InstancedMesh, one draw call, 1024-slot ring buffer, DOM text for damage numbers so it stays crisp instead of canvas-blurred, and a reset() that removes orphaned damage-number DOM nodes at match end.

Per-weapon reticles bloom off the ACTUAL spread the next shot will use (hud.js:1526-1540 calls the same K.effectiveSpread the sim calls), so the crosshair never lies. Shotgun gets a pellet-cone ring, sniper a fine dot plus drop hint, launcher an arc chevron.

gaps.gap: Firing your own weapon produces zero physical feedback. There is no camera kick, no view-model movement, no FOV punch and no screen shake on any of the six weapons.
gaps.evidence: `grep -rn "camShake *=" runtime/` returns exactly four lines: fx.js:36 (init 0), fx.js:133 (explosion), fx.js:161 (player hurt), fx.js:280 (decay). The shotFired listener at fx.js:88-93 spawns 6 particles and nothing else. player.js:1090 computes wantFov from scope/ads/sprint only. weapons.js:217 parents a static proto.clone() to the hand and never touches it again. The only reaction to firing is an aim-pitch nudge of 0.006-0.05 rad (0.34°-2.86°).
gaps.recommendation: In the shotFired handler, set W.camShake = Math.max(W.camShake, KICK[weaponId]) with a per-weapon table roughly proportional to the audio gains already tuned — smg ~0.045, ar ~0.07, pistol ~0.06, shotgun ~0.20, glauncher ~0.18, sniper ~0.26 — and only for a === W.player. In the same handler push a short FOV punch (+2° smg/ar, +5° shotgun/sniper) that decays over ~0.12s into the existing cam.fov lerp. Both are a handful of lines and they are the single highest-leverage change available on this dimension: with an SMG at 720 rpm the player pulls a trigger every 83ms and currently nothing on screen moves.

gaps.gap: No hitstop / sleep on kills, headshots or explosions — the most-cited technique in the canonical game-feel reference is entirely absent.
gaps.evidence: `grep -rn "hitstop|timeScale|slowmo|freeze" runtime/` returns only animation-mixer timeScale (player.js:958-987, freezing far actors' mixers for LOD) and the HUD pause comment. Nothing scales the frame dt on impact. Vlambeer's talk names sleep — pausing for a frame or a few when enemies die, the player is hit, or things explode — as a core buildup technique.
gaps.recommendation: Add a W.hitstopT that the frame loop honours by scaling dt (not by skipping the frame — keep rendering). 45-60ms on your own kill, 25-35ms on a headshot, 70ms on an explosion within 8m. CRITICAL CONSTRAINT: net.js runs a 12Hz broadcast and the host swaps silent guests for bots after 12s (hud.js:1964-1968 documents this), so in online matches scale only the CAMERA and FX update, never the sim step — or gate hitstop to single-player entirely. Even camera-only hitstop reads correctly.

gaps.gap: Explosions have no flash and no shockwave. A 95-damage grenade-launcher round with a 3.5m splash radius resolves as 40 coloured cubes and a low-passed noise thump.
gaps.evidence: fx.js:129-134 is the entire visual: burst of 26 fire cubes + 14 smoke cubes, then a camShake of up to 0.5 within 40m. `grep -rn "PointLight"` finds none in the royale FX path. There is no expanding ring, no additive flash sprite, no ground scorch. Sim (royale.js:64) rates the launcher at damage 95, splashR 3.5, and explode() applies knockback up to 7 m/s plus 4 m/s vertical — the physics say 'explosion', the visuals say 'confetti'.
gaps.recommendation: Two additions to the explosion handler, both reusing existing machinery. (1) An additive Sprite flash at the blast point, scale ramping 0→R*2.2 over ~90ms then fading — loot.js:189-204 already builds a radial canvas glow texture with AdditiveBlending you can reuse verbatim. (2) A pooled expanding ring: one THREE.RingGeometry mesh, additive, lying flat, scaling 0.2→R*1.6 over 250ms while alpha fades. Avoid a real PointLight — it forces shader recompiles across the scene on a browser GPU; the sprite reads as bright at bloom 0.14 anyway.

gaps.gap: Zero permanence. No bullet decals, no shell casings, no scorch marks, no corpses — after a firefight the world is bit-identical to before it.
gaps.evidence: `grep -rn "casing|decal|bulletHole" runtime/3d/` returns nothing. Bodies play a death clip then are silently removed by `setTimeout(..., 4500)` at player.js:1147 — no fade, no dissolve, no sink. Death loot (loot.js deathDrop) spawns items with no burst, no beam and no glow, while CHESTS get a glow sprite plus a vertical additive beam (loot.js:219-227) — so a killed player's loot is harder to spot than an untouched chest. Permanence is one of the three techniques Vlambeer names that this game ships none of.
gaps.recommendation: Cheapest-first. (1) Shell casings: reuse the existing particle pool in the shotFired handler — 1 cube per shot, brass 0xc9a227, size 0.045, gravity -9, ejected right-and-back, life 1.5s. Costs one spawn() call. (2) Bullet decals: a second InstancedMesh of ~64 camera-facing quads in a ring buffer, placed at the impact point offset along the surface normal, alpha-fading over ~20s. The impact event already carries the hit position; segmentColliders already returns nx/ny/nz (weapons.js:555), so the normal is free. (3) Give death-drop loot the same glow sprite chests get — that is a two-line change and it fixes a real gameplay legibility problem as well as a juice one.

gaps.gap: The victory moment is a text banner over a static world plus 60 CSS-transition div elements. There is no camera move, no world-space celebration, no slow-motion on the final kill.
gaps.evidence: hud.js:2039-2043 announceVictory shows a 34px Orbitron banner for 2600ms. hud.js:2133-2144 confetti() creates 60 absolutely-positioned 8x12px divs with a CSS `transition: top 2-4.5s linear` and removes them at 5000ms. audio.js:186-199 sting() plays four triangle-wave notes at 523/659/784/1046 Hz. During the 2600ms world hold (ffg_royale3d.js:333) the camera does nothing — the winner stands still in the third-person default at dist 4.2m while text sits over the top. This is the single most-screenshotted moment of the match.
gaps.recommendation: Spend the 2600ms you already hold. (1) Slow the last 0.4s before the banner to ~0.35x (single-player, or camera-only online). (2) Orbit the camera around the winner during the hold — lerp the existing camera yaw offset through ~120° and pull dist 4.2 → 5.5 with a slight upward pitch; player.js already owns the orbit params. (3) Fire the existing particle pool as world-space fireworks: three or four 30-cube bursts at +12m above the winner on a 400ms stagger, gold/blue/green, gravity -4. (4) Trigger the winner's existing cheer emote clip (it is already bound to N). All four reuse systems that exist; none needs a new subsystem.

gaps.gap: Enemies do not flash or react visually when hit. The only body confirmation is 4 particles at size 0.08 and a floating number.
gaps.evidence: fx.js:144-148: actorHurt spawns `n: 4` cubes at 0.08 size, life 0.35s, coloured 0x4aa8ff if the damage went to shield else 0xc23b3b. Nothing touches the victim's material. There is no flinch, no stagger, no hit reaction animation — `grep lastShotT runtime/3d/royale/player.js` shows the only combat-pose use is player.js:952 `const combat = a.input.ads || (W.t - a.lastShotT < 1.5)`, which is the SHOOTER's pose, not the victim's.
gaps.recommendation: Add a shared overlay: on actorHurt, set a per-actor flashT and in the actor update multiply the material colour toward white (or toward red for health damage, blue for shield) for ~70ms. Do NOT use emissive — player.js:184-221 documents that the Meshy GLBs' emissive was deliberately stripped because emissiveMap was a self-illum preview hack and the albedos were baked dark; raising emissive back would regress the fullbright bug that was already fixed this session. A colour multiply on material.color with a saved original is safe and cheap. Note the shield-vs-health colour split you already have in the particles is the right distinction to carry through.

gaps.gap: The hitmarker does not change on the killing blow, so the moment you actually kill someone is visually identical to the moment you chip them for 13.
gaps.evidence: hud.js:1812-1825: the hitMarker handler sets colour to #ffd54a on headshot else #ffffff, fontSize 34px else 26px, opacity 1 for 170/120ms. The kill is signalled only in audio (audio.js:269-271, a 700→1050 Hz two-tone) and by the ELIMINATED banner. Call of Duty and Warzone have used a distinct red X kill-confirm hitmarker for over a decade and it is one of the most imitated feedback conventions in shooters.
gaps.recommendation: In the actorDied listener, when killerId === W.player.id, immediately re-drive R.hitmark with a red (#ff4d4d) 40px glyph for ~280ms, overriding the head-priority latch (R._hitHeadUntil). Roughly six lines in a handler that already exists.

gaps.gap: Destructible props break silently on the visual channel. Barrels, trees and crates play a sound and vanish with no debris.
gaps.evidence: weapons.js:571 and :643 emit propBreak with {x, y, z, kind}. audio.js:286 listens and plays a two-blip break. fx.js has exactly nine listeners (shotFired, tracer, impact, explosion, swimState, swimStroke, actorHurt, actorDied, chestOpened) — propBreak is not among them. Destroying trees and rocks is literally Final Drop's advertised core loop, so this is the one comparison where I can point at a benchmark behaviour directly rather than inferring it.
gaps.recommendation: One listener, one burst call, keyed off `kind`: wood 0x9a7f4f / 0x6b5335 at n=14 with gravity, stone 0xa9a9a9 / 0x7d7d7d at n=12, barrel already gets the explosion path. Three lines. Also add hardLand and landed dust puffs (both events are already emitted and already have audio listeners, at audio.js:285 and :299) — n=6-10 dirt-coloured cubes at the feet scaled by impact speed.

gaps.gap: No weapon ever builds a recoil pattern — the kick fully re-centres between every shot, so the gun never fights you.
gaps.evidence: weapons.js:432 kicks input.pitch by 0.011 rad for the AR. weapons.js:254 recovers at `Math.min(a.recoilPitch, dt * 0.12)`, i.e. 0.12 rad/s. At the AR's 330 rpm the inter-shot interval is 0.18s, which recovers 0.0216 rad against an 0.011 rad kick; the SMG at 720 rpm recovers 0.010 rad against 0.006. Every weapon therefore fully resets before the next round, and a full-auto burst produces a ~0.6° wobble at ~5.5 Hz rather than a climb.
gaps.recommendation: Split the single kick into the two values commercial shooters use: a VISUAL kick that is large and fully recovers (feel), and an AIM kick that is small and only partly recovers (control). Concretely, keep recoilPitch as-is for the aim component but recover only ~70% of it, and add a separate camera-only pitch offset of 3-4x the current kick that recovers fast (~0.5 rad/s). This gets you a visible climb the player must fight without changing the effective spread model in sim/royale.js, which is shared with the crosshair bloom and would be a balance change rather than a feel change.

gaps.gap: The hurt vignette is binary — identical for a 5-damage graze and a 95-damage sniper hit — and there is no persistent low-HP state.
gaps.evidence: hud.js:1261 defines R.hurtTint as a red radial gradient at 0.4 alpha with a 0.3s transition; hud.js:1429 is the only driver: `R.hurtTint.style.opacity = W.t - p.lastDamageT < 0.7 ? "1" : "0"`. Nothing reads info.dmg or p.hp. The player has 100 HP + 100 shield (royale.js PLAYERK), so a sniper body shot at 105 damage and a distant pistol shot at ~10 produce the same screen.
gaps.recommendation: Scale opacity by damage — roughly clamp(dmg/60, 0.25, 1) — and add a second always-on tint whose opacity ramps once hp drops below 35, so the last third of your health bar is felt rather than read. A slow pulse on that low-HP tint (the lcPulse keyframe already exists at hud.js:58) plus a faint heartbeat via the existing thump() would cost almost nothing and is the standard shooter convention.

gaps.gap: Camera shake is per-frame white noise on position only, so it reads as buzz rather than impact and its character changes with framerate.
gaps.evidence: player.js:1079-1081: `cam.position.x += (Math.random() - 0.5) * W.camShake; cam.position.y += (Math.random() - 0.5) * W.camShake * 0.6;`. Fresh Math.random() every frame, no temporal coherence, no rotational component, linear decay at fx.js:280 (`dt * 1.8`). At 144fps this is a 144Hz jitter; at 30fps it is a visible stutter — the same camShake value produces a different sensation on different hardware, which matters in a browser game running on unknown machines.
gaps.recommendation: Drive x/y from a cheap smooth noise sampled on W.t (two sine sums at incommensurate frequencies is enough), add a small camera ROLL term (rotation.z) which is what actually sells impact, and square the decay (trauma^2 is the standard curve) so shake falls off sharply rather than lingering. Roughly ten lines in the block that already exists.

verdict: The storm architecture is genuinely BR-shaped and honestly scaled — 8 seeded phases over 12.9 min on standard, next-circle preview, escalating dps, warning beats, and a final circle that deliberately holds at 9.4 m instead of crowning a corpse — and that skeleton is at or above what a browser BR needs. The damage is in three tuning numbers and one missing layer: phase-1's wall closes at 8.2–10.5 m/s against a 9.6 m/s sprint, the ×3 storm ramp bypasses shields and makes the opening circle 2.3× more lethal than Fortnite's, and the whole 13-minute tension arc plays over one flat, unchanging music loop.
what_benchmarks_do: VERIFIED. Fortnite (gaming-tools.com storm table): 9 phases, waits 3:20/2:00/1:30/1:20/0:50/0:30/0/0/0, shrinks 3:00/2:00/1:30/1:10/1:00/1:00/0:55/0:45/0:45 — 1295 s ≈ 21.6 min total; dps ladder 1,1,2,5,8,10,10,10,10; "Storm Sickness" triples base damage only after SEVEN MINUTES in the storm. Fortnite OG hotfix flattened it further (1,1,1,1,1,2,5,8). Apex (apexlegends.wiki.gg / patch reporting): ring damage 2%/5%/10%/20%/20%/25% per tick, one tick per 1.5 s (≈1.33 %/s in ring 1 → ~75 s TTD); rings close in ≈3:15 each; max match ~19–20 min. PUBG (pubg.wiki.gg): 9 phases on Erangel, phase 1 = 120 s wait + 300 s shrink to 50% radius at 0.4 HP/s; final phase ~11%/s. CrazyGames' own developer docs: Action games average 13 min play time (D1 retention 8.1%), Shooting games 12 min. UNVERIFIED: Final Drop's actual circle count, phase timings, storm dps and match length are not published anywhere I could find — CrazyGames, final-drop.com and Miniplay all give only "up to 100 players", building, and looting. Any claim I make about Final Drop's specific pacing numbers would be invented, so I make none.
what_last_circle_does: Read from runtime/sim/royale.js STORM_PHASES + MODE and executed against the real Storm class (map half = 800×0.98 = 784 m, seed 42). STANDARD: 8 phases, totalS = 775 s = 12.92 min; start radius 1.35×half = 1058 m (larger than the 1600 m map, so the four corners start outside). Phase table (wait/shrink/radius/dps): 80/80 → 612 m /1; 60/70 → 455 m /1; 50/60 → 329 m /2; 45/50 → 220 m /3; 40/45 → 133 m /5; 30/40 → 71 m /7; 25/35 → 31 m /9; 20/45 → 9.4 m /12. Final circle holds at 9.4 m rather than closing to zero, enforced by royale.selftest.cjs ("storm: final circle holds small but non-zero at dps 12"), as is nesting ("every circle fully inside its predecessor") and determinism (same seed → identical circle plan). QUICK: 5 phases, totalS = 239 s = 3.98 min, pre-shrunk start at 0.75×half = 588 m, ground spawn, 25 starting shield, 1.8× loot. PRACTICE: no storm at all. Damage is a 1 Hz tick that RAMPS +50% per 6 s soaked (cap ×3) and bypasses shield entirely (storm.js: "storm ignores shield (classic BR): hp only"); soak decays −2 per safe tick. Measured TTD from 100 HP with the ramp: dps 1 → 43 s, dps 2 → 26 s, dps 3 → 20 s, dps 5 → 14 s, dps 12 → 8 s. Storm clock starts at deploy and includes the glide (spawn 240–270 m, chute auto-deploys at 110 m AGL, canopy descends at 5.5 m/s → ~28 s to land), so ground looting before the first wall moves is ~52 s. Tension scaffolding present: 10-second warning + siren, "THE STORM IS CLOSING" + siren, screen tint + thump on entering, minimap draws the live circle AND the next circle (white ring) plus a darkened outside veil, alive-count milestone announcements at 25/10/5/2 ("FINAL 2 — ONE KILL FROM THE WIN"), supply drops gated to phase ≥ 2 with a 3-phase gap so one lands ~phase 2 (t ≈ 160–290 s) and one ~phase 5 (t ≈ 495–580 s). Bots read st.nextCenter/nextRadius and score rotation urgency as needS = overM/8 + 6 against time left, escalating 40 → 70 → 95, with an unconditional ROTATE override once actually in the storm. Rotation tools without building: walk-in launch portals at POIs give +42 m/s vertical → ~80 m ballistic climb, then a fresh skydive with auto-canopy.
strengths: 8 phases on standard is a real BR shape, not a toy — Fortnite runs 9, PUBG 9, Apex 5-6. The escalating wait/shrink compression (80/80 → 20/45) mirrors the AAA structure of long early phases and rapid late ones.
12.92 min of storm is an honest scale-down of AAA (Fortnite 21.6 min, Apex ~19-20 min, PUBG ~30 min) rather than a copy — roughly 60% of the AAA length, which is the right direction for browser.

The final circle deliberately HOLDS at 9.4 m instead of closing to zero, with a selftest asserting it. Closing to zero storm-kills every survivor simultaneously and crowns a corpse; Fortnite and PUBG both do close to zero and rely on player density to resolve it. This is a better decision than the benchmark's, made deliberately and locked by a test.

The whole schedule is a pure deterministic function of (seed, mode, half) with stateAt(t) — host and clients agree with zero storm netcode. royale.selftest.cjs enforces determinism, circle nesting, and the phase-1 dps-0 grace. That is stronger engineering discipline than most browser BRs ship.

Next-circle preview is on the minimap (white ring + darkened outside veil) and the SAME nextCenter/nextRadius data drives bot rotation, so bots rotate to the next circle rather than the current one, with a real urgency model (needS = overM/8 + 6, scoring 40/70/95). That is AAA-shaped zone AI, not a beeline-to-center hack.

Tension beats exist and are layered: 10 s warning + siren, closing announcement + siren, screen tint on entering, and alive-count milestones at 25/10/5/2. Most browser BRs ship a bare countdown number and nothing else.

Supply-drop cadence is correctly placed as a mid-game and late-game re-engagement pulse (phase ≥ 2 with a 3-phase gap → ~t=160-290 s and ~t=495-580 s), matching the AAA pattern of one contested mid-game beat and one endgame kingmaker.
Storm damage soak decays asymmetrically in the player's favour (−2 per safe tick vs +1 per storm tick), so a dip through the wall stings but does not compound across a match.

The storm clock starts at deploy and includes the ~28 s glide, so there is no dead pre-storm timer padding the match — and practice mode has genuinely zero storm (dps 0, tToNext Infinity), verified by test.
Launch portals (+42 m/s → ~80 m climb → fresh skydive) give a real rotation tool that survives the no-building constraint — the functional equivalent of Fortnite launch pads for beating a bad circle.

gaps.gap: Quick mode's phase-1 wall closes faster than a player can sprint — by a factor of two on the trailing edge
gaps.evidence: Executed the real Storm class: quick P1 goes 588 m → 220 m in 35 s = 10.53 m/s of pure shrink, against SIM.MOVE.sprint = 9.6 m/s. Add the seeded center drift (seed 42: 7.84 m/s; worst case 8.42 m/s) and the trailing edge closes at 18.37 m/s — nearly 2× sprint, ~3.3× the 5.6 m/s swimSprint. The full radial gap of 368 m takes 38.4 s to sprint but the wall crosses it in 35 s. Storm dps 2 with the ramp kills a full-HP player in 26 s (measured). Quick is also a ground spawn, so there is no glide to pre-rotate with. The cause is structural: quick starts pre-shrunk at 0.75×half but its phase table still opens at radiusFrac 0.28 — one phase does the work standard spends four phases and 415 s on.
gaps.recommendation: Insert one intermediate step in STORM_PHASES.quick so the first cut is not 588→220. E.g. { wait: 25, shrink: 30, radiusFrac: 0.42, dps: 1 } ahead of the current first row, then let the existing 0.28 row follow. That yields ~7.7 m/s on the first wall and ~4.9 m/s on the second, both under sprint, and costs ~40 s (quick becomes ~4.6 min, closer to its own 5-minute label). Alternatively keep 5 phases and set P1 to radiusFrac 0.45 / shrink 45.

gaps.gap: Standard phase 1 leaves no rotation margin either — and none for water
gaps.evidence: Standard P1: 1058 m → 612 m over 80 s = 5.59 m/s wall; seed-42 center drift adds 2.64 m/s for 8.23 m/s of trailing-edge closure, and the worst-case drift (offset is rng()×0.8×Δr, so ~10% of seeds) reaches 4.47 m/s for 10.05 m/s total — above the 9.6 m/s sprint. Even the median case leaves a player on the far edge sprinting in a dead-straight line for the full 80 s with a 1.17× margin, no allowance for terrain, a firefight, or a heal (HEAL.speedMult 0.45 + blocksSprint). Anyone crossing water is caught outright: MOVE.swimSprint is 5.6 m/s, well below the wall. Every later phase is fine — P2-P8 close at 0.85-4.03 m/s worst case, comfortably under walk speed.
gaps.recommendation: Lengthen only P1's shrink from 80 s to 115 s (wall drops to 3.88 m/s, worst-case total 6.99 m/s — a 1.37× sprint margin) and cut P1's center-offset factor from 0.8 to 0.4 for the first phase only. Cost: 35 s on a 775 s match. This is the single highest-value pacing edit in the file.

gaps.gap: The damage ramp plus the shield bypass makes the opening storm 2.3× more lethal than Fortnite's, and the ramp arrives 23× sooner than the benchmark's
gaps.evidence: storm.js applies dps × min(3, 1 + floor(soakSeconds/6) × 0.5) directly to hp, skipping up to 100 points of shield. Measured TTD from 100 HP: dps 1 → 43 s (flat would be 100 s), dps 2 → 26 s, dps 3 → 20 s, dps 5 → 14 s. Fortnite's zone 1 at 1 dps takes 100 s and its 3× Storm Sickness multiplier only engages after seven minutes in the storm — Last Circle reaches the same 3× cap in 18 seconds. Apex ring 1 is 2% per 1.5 s tick ≈ 75 s. So the phase this game's opening storm most resembles is Fortnite's zone 6, not zone 1. Note the ramp itself is an explicit owner decision and correct in principle; the problem is that it stacks with a near-sprint-speed P1 wall and a shield bypass on the same phase.
gaps.recommendation: Keep the ramp, delay its onset: change the step from floor(soak/6) to floor(soak/12), or gate the ramp to st.phase >= 3. Either preserves 'it shouldn't stay 1/tick' in the phases where camping the wall is an actual strategy, while restoring a survivable ~70-80 s early grace that matches both benchmarks. (Leave the shield bypass alone — it is genuinely the classic BR convention.)

gaps.gap: The 13-minute tension arc plays over one flat, unchanging music loop, and the storm wall itself is silent
gaps.evidence: audio.js line 78: startMatchMusic() plays a single 'music_match.mp3' at 0.55 and never changes for the whole match; 'music_endgame.mp3' fires only in onMatchEnd(), i.e. AFTER the result is decided. The only storm audio is three one-shots — siren on stormWarning, siren on stormClosing, a 200 Hz thump on entering — and a per-tick blip. There is no continuous wall roar (nothing in audio.js subscribes to a storm-proximity signal), so the wall gives no directional or urgency cue at all. Every AAA BR escalates the mix as the ring closes and gives the wall a loud continuous bed; that escalation is the primary emotional carrier of the tension arc, and it is the one layer entirely absent here.
gaps.recommendation: Two changes, both cheap given the existing event bus. (1) On the 'stormPhase' event, ramp the match music: raise gain and add/unmute a percussion or drone layer as st.phase crosses 4 and 6, and switch to music_endgame.mp3 when aliveCount() <= 5 rather than at match end. (2) Add a looping filtered-noise bed whose gain is a function of (playerDistanceToWall) and panned toward the nearest wall point — storm.js already computes that distance every frame for the HUD tint (variable d in the playerInStorm block), so it is one emit away.

gaps.gap: There is nothing between a 12.9-minute match and a 4.0-minute one, and the 12.9-minute default consumes an entire average browser-shooter session
gaps.evidence: Verified totals: standard 775 s storm + ~28 s glide ≈ 13.4 min of wall-clock play for a winner (plus ~7 s lobby fill and up to 12 s drop-select). CrazyGames' own developer documentation states Action games average 13 minutes of play time and Shooting games 12 minutes. So one winning standard match IS the average session — a player who goes deep gets exactly one match and no second attempt, and the loop never gets its retention beat (CrazyGames explicitly recommends post-match as the ad/re-engagement moment). Meanwhile the alternative, quick at 3.98 min, is a different game: ground spawn, no glide, 1.8× loot. The 6-8 minute band where a browser BR default probably belongs is empty. The default mode is 'standard' (ffg_royale3d.js line 59).
gaps.recommendation: Add a third STORM_PHASES entry — 6 phases, glider drop, standard loot, ~7 min — as a new mode card, e.g. waits 55/45/35/30/25/20 with shrinks 60/55/45/40/35/40 and radiusFrac 0.70/0.48/0.30/0.17/0.08/0.012, dps 1/2/3/5/8/12 (≈ 440 s). Make it the default card in MODE_CARDS and demote standard to the 'long match' option. This is a table entry, a MODE row and a menu card — no new systems, no map picker involved.

gaps.gap: Nothing measures the alive-count decay curve, so the circle schedule is tuned blind
gaps.evidence: The storm timeline is a fixed function of (seed, mode, half) with no reference to Match.aliveCount() anywhere in royale.js or storm.js. Real BRs tune circle timings against a measured survivor curve; here the curve is produced entirely by 49 bot brains whose kill rate nobody has instrumented. royale.selftest.cjs tests the storm's determinism, nesting, damage and total length but contains no test of how many actors are alive at phase K. Two failure modes are structurally reachable and undetected: three players alive at t=300 s with 475 s of circle and a 329 m radius still to go (eight minutes of dead air in a 13-minute match), or twenty alive entering a 31 m phase-8 circle (the storm, not the players, decides it). I did not observe either — I am flagging that there is no instrument that would.
gaps.recommendation: Extend royale.selftest.cjs with a headless roster simulation — no rendering needed, just Match + Storm + a crude engagement model over the bot tier mix — that prints alive-count at each phase boundary across ~50 seeds and asserts a target band (e.g. 20-30 alive at phase 3, 8-14 at phase 5, 2-5 at phase 7). That turns the circle table from a guess into a fitted curve, and it is the prerequisite for tuning any of the recommendations above with confidence.

gaps.gap: The quick-mode menu card advertises a duration the storm does not have
gaps.evidence: hud.js MODE_CARDS: { id: 'quick', sub: '5-minute storm · double loot · hot start' }. The measured quick timeline is totalS = 239 s = 3.98 min. The player is told 5 minutes and gets 4 — and if the phase-1 fix above lands, the number changes again.
gaps.recommendation: Derive the card's subtitle from the table rather than hard-coding it: compute the mode's total from STORM_PHASES at menu-build time and render Math.round(total/60) + '-minute storm'. Then the label can never drift from the schedule again — fix the generator, not the string.

verdict: Ground movement is fundamentally sound and in several places better-modelled than the browser bar — 9.6 m/s sprint with a +13° FOV kick, a spread penalty graded continuously by speed (1.00× still → 1.45× walk → 1.72× sprint → 2× airborne), and a crouch capsule measured off the shipped animation clip (0.86×) instead of guessed. The gap is that there is not one skill-expressive traversal verb in the game: no slide, no mantle, no momentum carry off a jump — which is precisely the layer Epic shipped (slide C3S1, mantle + sprint C3S2) specifically because Zero Build removed building, and Last Circle has removed building permanently.
what_benchmarks_do:
FINAL DROP (verified, crazygames.com/game/final-drop control list, quoted verbatim): "WASD = movement / Space = jump / C = crouch / Shift = toggle run / walk". Four ground verbs, and SHIFT is a TOGGLE there too — the owner's sprint-toggle direction matches the primary benchmark exactly. No slide, vault, swim, or glide verb is advertised. Its traversal expression comes from on-demand walls/floors/ramps (building), which Last Circle has removed. No speed figures are published for Final Drop; I could not verify its m/s, acceleration, or jump height, and I am not inventing them.

FORTNITE (verified, pockettactics.com/fortnite/map-speed): jog 2 m/s, run 5.48 m/s, sprint 6.47 m/s, swim 5.49 m/s, swim-jump 8.75 m/s; sprint drains an Energy/stamina bar (Fortnite Wiki). Slide added Chapter 3 Season 1; mantling + tactical sprint added C3S2, and multiple guide sources state mantling was introduced alongside Zero Build so players could climb obstacles without building.

APEX LEGENDS (search-summary of apexlegends.wiki.gg, second-hand): walk 3.8 m/s, sprint 5.7 m/s, crouch-walk 1.75 m/s; holding a weapon −13%; a regen item costs −40% speed and blocks sprint. Slide, slide-jump and wall-climb are core (widely known; not verified from a primary source this session).

PUBG (verified, pubg.wiki.gg/wiki/Movement_Speed): sprint 6.3, run 4.7, walk 1.7, crouch-sprint 4.8, crouch-run 3.4, prone crawl 1.2, swim 2.9 m/s. Vaulting and climbing shipped in 2018; prone and lean are stance verbs Last Circle does not have.

Net: every AAA benchmark sprints at 5.7–6.5 m/s and buys depth with a movement-tech layer (slide/mantle/climb/prone/stamina). None of them are faster than Last Circle in raw m/s.
what_last_circle_does:
Constants (runtime/sim/royale.js:103-128): walk 6.0, sprint 9.6, ADS 3.8, swim 4.0, swim-sprint 5.6 m/s; jumpV 7.8, gravity −22, accelT 0.13 s, airControl 0.4. Derived: jump apex = 7.8²/44 = 1.383 m, airtime = 2×7.8/22 = 0.709 s; sprint:walk ratio 1.6. CROUCH {speedMult 0.45 → 2.7 m/s, heightMult 0.86, eyeMult 0.60, spreadMult 0.62}. HEAL {speedMult 0.45, blocksSprint true} → 2.7 m/s and no sprint while drinking. Wading (in water, not swimming) ×0.55 → 3.3 m/s. Capsule: radius 0.45, height 1.8, eye 1.62, swimDepth 1.1. STEP_UP 0.55 m auto-step (player.js:581).

Verbs actually implemented (player.js stepActor): walk; sprint (SHIFT latch, forward-only — gated on inp.mz > 0.5, latch auto-drops when you stop moving forward, player.js:566); crouch (hold C, ground-only, and sprint always wins — player.js:779); jump; swim with a SPACE stroke-hop that multiplies horizontal velocity ×1.6 (player.js:809) and real axis-separated collision against hulls/piers; wade; skydive (15 m/s horizontal, −20 m/s fall, −34 with SHIFT dive) from 240–270 m over a player-chosen LZ (setDropTarget, player.js:421); parachute (8.5 m/s horizontal, −5.5 descent = 1.55:1 glide ratio) with SPACE toggling deploy/cut-away as often as you like, auto-deploy at 110 m first time, 22 m hard floor after; mid-air re-chute above 12 m AGL (player.js:829) so stepping off a sky island is an escape; launch portals (vel.y = 42, half-gravity ascent = 42²/24.2 ≈ 73 m, then hands over to the skydive); ramps and interior/exterior stair-ramps as level geometry.

Camera: third-person at 4.2 m, ADS pulls to 1.7 m over the right shoulder, scoped sniper goes true first-person (0.02) and hides the player model; base FOV 57 (user 50–85), sprint kicks it to 70 (player.js:1090); crouch eye-dip is lerped at 12/s rather than snapped.

Absent (repo-wide grep over runtime/ for slide|vault|mantle|zipline|grapple|prone|lean|knocked|downed returns only audio.js:258 "slide rack" and a torso-lean pose constant): no slide, no mantle/vault, no climb, no prone, no lean, no stamina, no ziplines, no vehicles, no fall damage (hardLand at vy < −16 fires audio only, audio.js:311), no bunny-hop or air-strafe speed gain.

Scale check: 1600 m square map (maps.js:23), so a full cross at 9.6 m/s is 167 s; the storm's fastest closing edge is ~5.6 m/s in phase 1 and ~1.1 m/s late, so sprint always outruns it.
strengths: Sprint TOGGLE is not a compromise — it is what the primary benchmark ships. Final Drop's own control list reads "Shift = toggle run / walk" (verified verbatim from crazygames.com). Last Circle also solves the classic toggle problem properly: the HUD sprint pip goes bright when you are genuinely sprinting and DIM when the latch is on but you are not (ADS, airborne, walking backwards), so the indicator never lies about your real speed (hud.js:1347-1358), and the latch auto-drops when you stop moving forward (player.js:566) so you never wander into a fight sprinting from three minutes ago.

The spread economy makes movement a real decision instead of a binary. effectiveSpread grades the penalty continuously by speed: 1.00× standing, 1.20× crouch-walk (2.7 m/s), 1.45× walk (6.0), 1.72× sprint (9.6), ×2 airborne, ×0.62 crouched, and a 0.15× first-shot bonus for a deliberate shot from a standstill (royale.js:152-172). Most browser BRs use a binary moving/not-moving flag; this is AAA intent, and the node selftest holds it honest (royale.selftest.cjs:231-244).

Raw speed beats every AAA benchmark and the FOV kick makes it read: 9.6 m/s sprint is +48% on Fortnite (6.47), +52% on PUBG (6.3), +68% on Apex (5.7), with base FOV 57 kicking to 70 while sprinting. For a browser BR where sessions are short and rotations should not be a chore, that is the right call, not an accident.

Heal-while-moving is costed almost exactly like Apex: HEAL.speedMult 0.45 (−55%) + blocksSprint, against Apex's verified −40% + no sprint. You can still reposition behind cover at 2.7 m/s, you just cannot run. Crouch at 0.45× walk (2.7 m/s) also lands on Apex's crouch ratio (1.75/3.8 = 0.46).

Hitbox honesty most shipped games do not bother with: CROUCH.heightMult 0.86 was MEASURED off the shipped Meshy crouch clip (head bone 1.36 m + 0.18 m capsule overhead = 1.54 m), and actorHeight() only shrinks the capsule for an actor that actually has the crouch clip loaded (royale.js:114-134) — a skin whose clip failed to bake keeps its full capsule rather than eating shots through a visible head.

The parachute is a genuine traversal verb, not a cutscene: SPACE toggles deploy and cut-away freely, and SPACE in mid-air above 12 m AGL re-opens it (player.js:829). Combined with the launch portals (vel.y 42 → ~73 m ballistic → skydive) this gives the map real vertical rotation without vehicles or ziplines — the correct browser-scale substitute.

Swimming has real collision. The swim branch runs the same axis-separated blockedHoriz test as the ground branch with a +0.45 m step allowance (player.js:812-822), so you stop dead on a shipwreck hull but can haul out onto a low deck. Most browser games let you swim through geometry. Swim 4.0 / 5.6 m/s also beats PUBG's verified 2.9, and the ×1.6 SPACE stroke-hop mirrors Fortnite's swim-jump (5.49 → 8.75, a 1.59× boost).

gaps.gap: No slide — the game has zero skill-expressive traversal verbs, and this is the single biggest movement gap versus every benchmark
gaps.evidence: Repo-wide grep over runtime/ for \bslid(e|ing)\b|\bvault\b|\bmantle|zipline|grapple returns only audio.js:258 ("slide rack" reload foley) and pose.js torso "lean" — no movement verb exists. Slide is core to Apex and Warzone, and Fortnite added slide in Chapter 3 Season 1 followed by mantle + sprint in C3S2; multiple guides state mantling was introduced specifically so Zero Build players could traverse without building. Last Circle removed building permanently, so it took the Zero Build constraint without taking the Zero Build compensation. There is also a live UX symptom: a.crouching is false whenever sprint is latched and W is held (player.js:779), so with the sprint TOGGLE on you cannot crouch mid-push without first un-toggling — an extra keypress in a firefight.
gaps.recommendation: Add sprint+C → slide in stepActor: enter at current speed (9.6 m/s), decay to CROUCH speed (2.7) over ~0.6 s, hold the crouch capsule (heightMult 0.86) and crouch spread (0.62×) for the duration, ~1.0 s cooldown before re-sliding, cancel on jump. This does not touch the sprint toggle (it reads the latch), needs no new animation beyond re-timing the existing crouch clip, and is testable from royale.selftest.cjs as a pure speed/height curve. It also resolves the crouch-while-latched awkwardness: sprint+C becomes slide-into-crouch, which is what the player wanted anyway.

gaps.gap: No mantle/vault — anything between the 0.55 m auto-step and the 1.38 m jump apex requires a precise jump, and anything above 1.38 m is an impassable wall
gaps.evidence: STEP_UP = 0.55 (player.js:581); jump apex = jumpV²/(2·|gravity|) = 7.8²/44 = 1.383 m. Between those two values traversal is a timing test with no assist; above 1.383 m the geometry is simply a wall, so windowsills, crates, fence lines and low walls are all routed around rather than crossed. PUBG shipped vault+climb in 2018; Fortnite shipped mantle with Zero Build; Apex has climb. Final Drop's advertised control list has none of these, so this is a gap against AAA, not against the primary bar.
gaps.recommendation: Add a hold-jump mantle for ledges between 0.55 m and ~1.6 m: on jump input with a collider top in that band within ~0.8 m ahead, snap the actor onto the top over ~0.35 s with movement locked. Reuse supportAt/blockedHoriz — no new collision code. Do this AFTER slide; it is the second-order win.

gaps.gap: Airborne velocity decays toward ZERO, not toward your input — a jump with no key held bleeds ~89% of your speed, so there is no momentum carry off any ledge or jump
gaps.evidence: player.js:798 — k = airControl · min(1, dt/accelT) = 0.4 · dt/0.13, applied against a target of (0,0) when no key is held (tx/tz are multiplied by the has-input flag at :796-797). That is a 0.325 s decay time constant against a 0.709 s airtime: (1−0.4·0.0167/0.13)^42.5 ≈ 0.11 of your entry speed left on landing. Holding W masks it, but stepping/jumping off anything sideways or backwards, or releasing keys to look around mid-air, applies air-braking that exists in no benchmark — Apex, Fortnite and Quake-lineage shooters all conserve horizontal momentum in the air.
gaps.recommendation: In the airborne branch, steer velocity toward the input direction at the current speed instead of decaying it toward zero: when |input| ≈ 0 in the air, skip the velocity lerp entirely (gravity still applies). One-line-scale change in stepActor, restores momentum carry, and is a prerequisite for slide feeling good (a slide that ends in a jump must keep its speed).

gaps.gap: Landing has zero visual feedback — 50 touchdowns a match and every jump land silently on screen
gaps.evidence: Grep of fx.js for landed|hardLand|dip returns nothing (only camShake plumbing at :36/:133/:161/:280), while both events are emitted (player.js:696 "landed", :854 "hardLand" at vy < −16) and audio.js DOES handle them (:311 hardLand thump, :325 own-landing thump). So the impact is audible but invisible: no dust ring, no water splash, no camera dip. There is also no head-bob or view-punch anywhere in the camera path (updateCamera, player.js:1032-1094) — the only movement-driven camera cue in the game is the sprint FOV kick. This is already listed in GAP_SCAN.md:37/167 and FIX_QUEUE.json:602, so it may be in flight.
gaps.recommendation: In fx.js wireEvents, add a `landed` handler (dust ring, or water ring when a.pos.y <= W.map.waterY + 0.4, reusing the existing burst()) and a `hardLand` handler (bigger burst + a short camShake scaled by impact speed, which is already passed as the second arg). Self-contained in fx.js; no player.js change.

gaps.gap: Bots never crouch — the crouch verb is player-only, so every enemy silhouette is full-height 1.8 m and no bot ever takes the 0.62× spread bonus
gaps.evidence: Grep of bots.js for the input struct shows inp.sprint set at :347/:355/:407/:556/:560 and inp.jump at :412/:414/:563, but no inp.crouch anywhere in the file. Combat behaviour is strafe + jump (tier ≥ 3 jumps at ~0.35/s, :563), never a crouch-peek. Half the tactical value the crouch system was built for — smaller capsule, tighter cone — never appears on the receiving end, so the player is never taught to counter it and the top bot tiers leave accuracy on the table.
gaps.recommendation: In the combat state, have tier ≥ 3 bots set inp.crouch when holding a firing position at range (dist > prefer and ground speed < 1.5), and drop it when repositioning. Roughly a 5-line addition next to the existing strafe logic; it also makes the expert tiers measurably more accurate via the existing CROUCH.spreadMult.

gaps.gap: No crouch-toggle option even though sprint and ADS both have one — holding C for a long fight is awkward on a browser keyboard
gaps.evidence: player.js:570 reads crouch as pure hold state (inp.crouch = !!keys.KeyC), while hud.js:2232 exposes toggles for exactly two actions: [["Sprint (SHIFT)", "sprintToggle"], ["Aim down sights", "adsToggle"]]. The comment at player.js:568 already reasons about browser-keyboard ergonomics (C instead of Ctrl, because Ctrl+W closes the tab) — the same reasoning applies to holding the key.
gaps.recommendation: Add a third row to that settings array: ["Crouch (C)", "crouchToggle"], with a latch mirroring _sprintLatch, cleared in resetInputState() alongside the others. Roughly 6 lines across player.js and hud.js.

gaps.gap: Sprint has no cost outside of accuracy — no stamina, no weapon-raise on sprint exit, no fire lockout — so W-key-forever is strictly optimal whenever you are not shooting
gaps.evidence: sprinting = inp.sprint && inp.mz > 0.5 with no resource gate (player.js:786); the only penalty is the 1.72× spread while firing (royale.js:164), and firing during sprint is allowed with no ready-up delay. Fortnite gates sprint behind an Energy bar; Apex/Warzone charge a weapon-raise on sprint exit. Against 1600 m of map and a storm whose fastest edge closes at ~5.6 m/s versus your 9.6, this means traversal carries no decision at all.
gaps.recommendation: LOWEST priority, and only if slide ships first — a stamina bar would fight the sprint toggle and would be wrong for a browser arcade BR. If anything, add a short (~0.18 s) weapon-ready delay when transitioning out of sprint into fire, which preserves the toggle and rotation speed while giving sprint a real tactical cost. Do not add stamina.

verdict: Last Circle's bot AI is the most architecturally serious part of the game and comfortably out-designs the documented bot behaviour of Fortnite and PUBG: a utility-scored 9-state brain per bot, 5 skill tiers (700ms/7.5° down to 210ms/0.9°), 6 personalities, LOS-gated perception with swept collision, a human aim-error model with acquire overshoot and target-motion penalties, burst discipline, reload-break-for-cover, disengage-to-heal, fight fatigue, and gunshot hearing at 250m — all 49 bots fully simulated, no LOD fakery. But the difficulty curve is badly deflated by two one-line facts: bots never drink shields until they are already hurt (so they roam at 100 EHP against the player's 200) and their aim point of feet+1.15m sits 0.4m below the head hitbox threshold, so they physically cannot land a headshot at any tier — together roughly a 4-6x TTK advantage to the human — and there is no difficulty scaling of any kind, which is exactly the layer Fortnite and Warzone build around their much dumber bots.
what_benchmarks_do: VERIFIED — Fortnite: bots added Chapter 2 Season 1 alongside SBMM; per Fortnite Wiki/community docs they "pick up weapons and items, and harvest materials" but "cannot build complex structures or use advanced tactics like editing quickly or rotating strategically", have "usually inaccurate aim, but immense detection range as they can start shooting at you from very far away so long as they have direct line of sight", "move in straight lines or stand still while shooting", and "rarely use healing items smartly". Bot share is set by SBMM: 70-90% of the lobby in low-skill matches, near zero at high skill. VERIFIED — PUBG: casual mode is majority bots (~12 real players, rest AI); bots "loot, shoot, grenade, and move throughout the map to mimic a real player" but are "generally easy to beat" and players complain the mix of "old dumb bots and newer aggressive ones creates weird pacing". VERIFIED — Warzone: Season 3 (March 2025) added Battle Royale Casual, a mostly-bot lobby aimed at newcomers. VERIFIED — Apex Legends: no AI fill bots at all; "bot lobby" is slang for low-skill human lobbies, and the Season 20 (Dec 2024) matchmaking overhaul closed the smurf route. UNVERIFIED — Final Drop: the CrazyGames page (verified: browser/desktop-only, iframe-hosted, released June 2026, 9.2/10 over the last 6 months, "up to 100 players", building enabled) and final-drop.com contain NO statement about bots, bot fill, matchmaking, or AI difficulty, and I found no Reddit/dev source that documents them. I cannot say what Final Drop's bots do, or whether it has any. The comparison below is therefore against a verified AAA baseline plus an inferred browser-BR baseline, not against measured Final Drop behaviour.
what_last_circle_does: Per-bot BRAIN = utility-scored state machine over a blackboard, writing only into the same input struct the human uses (bots.js:8-11) — so bots are bound by identical movement, spread and weapon code. 49 bots + 1 human in standard mode (royale.js:284, ffg_royale3d.js:271-289); online multiplayer caps at 8 humans (net.js:5), so 42+ of 50 slots are bots even in a full friend lobby — bots ARE the lobby. STATES (9): DROP/LOOT/ROTATE/ENGAGE/FLEE/HEAL/CAMP/PUSH/WANDER, re-scored on a stagger of 0.15s within 120m of the player and 0.4s beyond (bots.js:113-116); act() runs every frame for all 49. TIERS: BOT_TIERS = 700ms/7.5°, 500/4.5, 380/2.8, 300/1.8, 210/0.9 (royale.js:297-303), mixed [8,12,14,10,5] = 49 for standard (royale.js:304) — so a lobby has 8 near-helpless bots and 5 roughly pro-reaction ones. PERSONALITIES (6): rusher, flanker, camper, loot_goblin, rotator, sniper (royale.js:305), driving drop choice (85% POI for rushers/rotators vs 55%, loot_goblins take the farthest POIs — bots.js:82-91), ENGAGE bonus (+15 rusher), CAMP eligibility (camper/sniper only, sniper camps at 0.55R vs 0.8R), PUSH-toward-gunfire eligibility, and strafe pattern (flankers hold one strafe direction = a circling arc, at 0.8 vs 0.4 lateral input beyond 50m). PERCEPTION: 160° cone out to 200m, anyone within 15m registers regardless of facing, a heard shooter registers 360° for 4s, gated by map.losBlocked — a genuine swept segment-vs-collider test plus a terrain heightfield march (maps.js:1201-1236), so bots cannot see or shoot through walls or ramps. Target stickiness bias 0.6, memory decay at 8s. HEARING: every shot broadcasts to brains within 250m with the shooter's id (bots.js:36-42). AIM ERROR MODEL: tier base × acquire overshoot (3× decaying over 0.6s) × target-motion penalty (up to 1.55×, +0.35 if the target is airborne) × 0.55 tightening in a final-4 duel, wandered as a smooth ~2s sine wobble rather than white noise (bots.js:587-597). Reaction gate = tier reactionMs before the first shot. Projectile lead for weapons under 600 m/s; a bisection ballistic solve for the arcing grenade launcher (speed 26, gravity -18, +3 launch boost) so bot-fired shells actually land (bots.js:326-341). FIRE DISCIPLINE: AR bursts ~4 rounds then pauses 0.35-0.75s (≈57% duty cycle), SMG/pistol 8, sniper only fires below 1.5 m/s, ADS beyond 25m, engagement range capped at falloff[1]×1.3 (156m for an AR). COMBAT MICRO: preferred ranges by class (shotgun 7m, SMG 14, pistol 16, AR 30, sniper 90, GL 26), close/retreat bands, per-0.5-1.4s strafe flips, tier-3+ bots jump-spam at ~0.35/s, and reloading triggers a sprinting lateral+backward break instead of standing in the open (bots.js:552-559). DISENGAGE LOGIC: 14s of stalemate with no damage taken and >6 alive breaks the fight and adds a 6s avoid-cooldown on that target (bots.js:527-531); a suppression reflex sprints 18m laterally when shot by someone unseen (bots.js:383-391); FLEE blends the escape vector 55/45 toward the next circle centre so bots never run into the storm (bots.js:266-281). INVENTORY: weapon re-selected every think by sustained DPS × pellets + rarity×20 with dry-gun detection and a 1.15× hysteresis (bots.js:471-497), plus bot-only trade-up at the 3-gun cap (loot.js:381-391). Loot scoring: chest 72 ungeared/55 geared, weapon 66+6r ungeared/30+8r geared, shield 45, other consumable 34, ammo 38, minus 0.4/metre, skipping anything give() would refuse. Chests obey the same 2s channel as the player. STORM: taking storm damage is a hard override to ROTATE; otherwise rotation urgency = (metres past the next radius)/8 + 6s of margin vs time remaining (halved while the wall is closing) scoring 95/70/40. HUMAN TELLS: 68 gamertag-style names (royale.js:307-318), zero "BOT" labelling anywhere in the HUD (grep isBot in hud.js → 0 hits), and a 30% chance to dance or cheer on a kill when no new threat is in sight (bots.js:29-34). Stuck detection accumulates only after a state has expressed movement intent, jumping at 0.7s and rerouting at 2.2s.
strengths: Perception is honest in a way most BR bots are not. Bots are LOS-gated by the same swept segment-vs-collider test the bullets use (maps.js:1201-1236) plus a terrain march — they cannot see or shoot through a wall or a ramp. Fortnite's documented bots have 'immense detection range' with LOS but no meaningful range cap; Last Circle caps sight at 200m and engagement at falloff[1]x1.3.

The aim-error model is genuinely good craft, not a random-number difficulty knob: tier base error multiplied by a 3x acquire overshoot decaying over 0.6s, a target-motion penalty up to 1.55x plus 0.35x for airborne targets, and — critically — wandered as a smooth ~2s sine (bots.js:595-597) rather than per-shot white noise, so a sustained burst sweeps a coherent arc across a strafing target. That is what human tracking actually looks like.

The skill spread is wide enough to read as a real lobby rather than one difficulty setting: 8 bots at 700ms/7.5deg are visibly bad, 5 at 210ms/0.9deg are at human-pro reaction time (royale.js:297-304). Most browser BRs ship one bot.

Behaviours that AAA bots demonstrably lack. Fortnite bots 'move in straight lines or stand still while shooting' and 'rarely use healing items smartly'; Last Circle bots strafe on 0.5-1.4s flips, sprint laterally out of the open the moment a reload starts (bots.js:552-559), break off a 14s stalemate and blacklist that target for 6s, and disengage to heal at sub-50 combined HP while blending the escape vector toward the next circle so they never flee into the storm.

Bots hear. Every shot broadcasts to brains within 250m carrying the shooter's id, granting 360-degree awareness of that specific shooter for 4s, and rusher/rotator/flanker personalities push toward the noise (bots.js:36-42, 182). This is what makes third-partying happen and is the main reason mid-game feels populated.

Weapon handling is competent rather than decorative: guns are re-scored every think by damage x pellets x rpm/60 + rarity x 20 with dry-gun detection, so a bot switches off an empty rifle instead of pulling a dead trigger, and the pellet term stops a legendary shotgun scoring below the starter pistol. Bots at the 3-gun cap can also trade up (loot.js:381-391), which is what keeps chest and supply-drop rolls from being wasted on 49 of 50 actors.

The grenade launcher gets a real ballistic solution — a 24-iteration bisection on a closed-form range that accounts for the +3 launch boost the textbook formula misses (bots.js:326-341). Almost nobody bothers; without it every bot holding one is harmless.

All 49 bots are genuinely simulated every frame, with only the think cadence staggered (0.15s near / 0.4s far). There is no off-screen fake attrition, so the kill feed and the alive counter reflect an actual fight happening across the map.

The disguise is complete at the UI layer: 68 believable gamertags and zero isBot references in hud.js — nothing labels a bot as a bot, and kill taunts (30% dance/cheer after a kill with no live threat) are the kind of detail that sells the illusion.
Bot brains re-attach to a slot when an online guest disconnects mid-match (net.js:222-229), so a friend rage-quitting does not leave a statue in the endgame.

gaps.gap: Bots never shield up proactively, so they fight the entire early and mid game at 100 EHP against the player's 200.
gaps.evidence: bots.js:165 — s.HEAL = (a.hp < 45 || (a.shield < 30 && a.hp < 80)) && heals && !bb.target ? 75 : (a.hp < 60 && heals && W.t - a.lastDamageT > 6 ? 45 : 0). Every actor spawns at hp 100 / shield 0 (royale.js:92 START_LOADOUT carries no shield). At hp=100, shield=0 the first clause is false and the second clause requires hp<80, so a completely healthy bot carrying six mini shields scores HEAL = 0 and never drinks them. LOOT scores 64 while ungeared, so it keeps scavenging instead. Bots only ever shield AFTER they are already hurt, at which point startHeal (bots.js:314) correctly prioritises big_shield when shield<40.
gaps.recommendation: Add a low-priority top-off branch: when out of combat (no bb.target, >6s since lastDamageT) and shield < 100 with a shield consumable in inventory, score HEAL ~30 — above WANDER (12) and geared LOOT (20-35) but below ROTATE and any live fight. This alone roughly doubles bot effective HP and is the single largest difficulty lever in the file. Consider gating it by tier so tier-1/2 bots stay sloppy about it — that is a believable skill tell, and it preserves the low end of the curve.

gaps.gap: Bots are mathematically incapable of landing a headshot, at every tier — their aim point sits below the head hitbox.
gaps.evidence: bots.js:567 aims at aimY = tp.y + 1.15. The head zone requires py > feetY + (headY - feetY) * 0.86 AND horizontal distance < 0.2m (weapons.js:522), which with actorHeight 1.8 means above 1.548m — 0.4m above the bot's aim point. Bot pitch error is only cos(errPhase*0.83) * err * 0.6; for a tier-5 bot (0.9 deg) at 30m that is ~0.28m of vertical wander, so it cannot reach the head band even at the top of its wobble. Meanwhile the human hitting heads gets headMult 1.5 (2.5 on the sniper: 105 base becomes 262, an instant kill through a full 200 EHP bar). Combined with the shield gap above, a human with a legendary AR kills a bot in ~2.5 body shots (0.45s) while a tier-5 bot needs ~1.5-2.3s of tracked fire through a 57% burst duty cycle — call it a 4-6x TTK asymmetry in the player's favour on every clean engagement.
gaps.recommendation: Bias the aim point upward by tier: keep +1.15 for tiers 1-2, raise toward +1.45 for tier 3, +1.55 for tiers 4-5 so the top tiers land occasional headshots through natural wobble. Do NOT give bots a deterministic head-aim — the goal is that the 5 scary bots in the lobby occasionally delete you, not that all 49 do.

gaps.gap: No difficulty scaling of any kind — no player-facing setting, no SBMM analogue, no dynamic adjustment. Every player gets the identical seeded tier mix on their first match and their five-hundredth.
gaps.evidence: grep -rni "difficulty" over runtime/ returns zero hits. The mix is fixed at BOT_TIER_MIX.standard = [8,12,14,10,5] (royale.js:304) and drawn deterministically from the match seed in attachBrain (bots.js:51-58). This is precisely the layer both AAA benchmarks build around bots that are behaviourally far worse than these: Fortnite ties bot share to SBMM (70-90% of the lobby at low skill, near zero at high), and Warzone shipped a whole mostly-bot Battle Royale Casual mode in March 2025 for newcomers.
gaps.recommendation: Cheapest high-value version: persist a local skill estimate (rolling average placement and kills over the last ~10 matches) and shift the tier mix along it — a new player draws something like [16,16,11,5,1], a veteran [3,7,14,15,10]. It is a single weighted array swap at attachBrain and needs no new AI code. A visible Casual/Standard/Sweat selector in the lobby is the fallback if you would rather not hide it, but the invisible version is what the benchmarks actually do and it is what keeps the first ten matches winnable without making match fifty trivial.

gaps.gap: No pathfinding at all — straight-line steering plus a stuck timer — so bots cannot reliably enter buildings and cannot reach elevated loot, which is both a difficulty deflator and the game's loudest bot tell.
gaps.evidence: grep for navmesh/pathfind/astar over runtime/3d/royale/ returns zero hits. moveToward (bots.js:402-419) points at the target, hops when supportAt 1.4m ahead is 0.55-2.2m above the feet (jump apex is actually only 7.8^2/(2*22) = 1.38m), and on stuckT > 2.2 rerouts to randNear(a, 25) — a random point, not an attempt to find the door. Meanwhile loot is placed inside huts through a single 1.4m door gap on one face (maps.js:531-546), on every floor of multi-storey towers at fy+0.5 (maps.js:585), on tower roofs (maps.js:590), and on elevated points at +9.9m and +29.6m and on sky islands (maps.js:909, 930, 1131). A bot that approaches a hut from the wrong side grinds the wall, jumps, strafes randomly, then abandons the loot after 2.2s; upper tower floors and roof chests are effectively unreachable.
gaps.recommendation: Two tiers of fix. Cheap (S/M, do this first): give POIs and structures a small set of hand-tagged approach waypoints — door mouths, ramp bases — and have onEnter route bot moveTo through the nearest waypoint when the target is inside a structure footprint; also change the stuck reroute from randNear to 'step to the nearest waypoint of the thing I was trying to reach'. Full (L): a coarse walkable-cell grid baked per map at build time with A* — 1600m at 8m cells is 200x200, well within budget, and it would fix the wall-grinding tell permanently. Until then, buildings remain a reliable exploit: the player is safe indoors from most of the lobby.

gaps.gap: Bots never contest supply drops — the only legendary source in the game lands uncontested unless the player happens to be standing there.
gaps.evidence: loot.js emits supplyDropSpawned and supplyDropLanded (loot.js:258, 276) and the only subscribers are audio.js:310/321 and hud.js:1888/1893 — bots.js subscribes to actorDied and shotFired only (bots.js:29, 36). loot.js's own comment at line 379 names this: 'supply drops, the only legendary source, contested by nobody.' rollSupplyDrop weights are [0,0,10,35,55] toward epic/legendary (royale.js:292).
gaps.recommendation: Subscribe brains to supplyDropSpawned, write it to the blackboard, and score a LOOT override of ~70 for bots within ~150m whose personality is rusher/loot_goblin/rotator, decaying with distance and expiring ~45s after landing. Half a dozen lines. Supply drops are the best-scripted drama moment a BR has and right now they generate none.

gaps.gap: Bots never crouch — they cannot use the game's own accuracy mechanic, and they never present the smaller hitbox.
gaps.evidence: grep -c crouch runtime/3d/royale/bots.js → 0. inp.crouch is never written by any brain. Crouch is worth CROUCH.spreadMult 0.62 (a 38% tighter cone) plus a movement-penalty drop, and shrinks the capsule to heightMult 0.86 for actors with the clip baked (royale.js:123, 132-134). Snipers in CAMP state just stand upright and rotate yaw at 0.25 rad/s (bots.js:507-516).
gaps.recommendation: Set inp.crouch = true in actCamp, and in actEngage for sniper/camper personalities when dist > 40 and the bot is holding position. Cheap, immediately visible, and it makes the CAMP state read as a player holding an angle rather than a mannequin spinning in place.

gaps.gap: No true cover-seeking — bots strafe and dodge but never query the world for geometry that would break line of sight.
gaps.evidence: The header comment at bots.js:3 claims bots 'use cover', but the only implementations are a strafe flip every 0.5-1.4s (bots.js:548-551), a lateral+backward sprint while reloading (bots.js:552-559), and a suppression reflex that picks a point 18m away at the attacker's bearing +/- 1.2 rad with no check that anything there actually blocks LOS (bots.js:383-391). Nothing ever calls losBlocked to find a position where the enemy cannot see it.
gaps.recommendation: Add a cheap cover query: sample ~8 points on a 6-12m ring around the bot, keep those where map.losBlocked(candidate eye, target eye) is true and the bot can reach them, pick the nearest. Use it for the suppression reflex, for reload breaks, and for FLEE. It reuses machinery that already exists and is the difference between 'strafes a lot' and 'plays cover'.

gaps.gap: Sniper bots never lead a moving target, while AR bots do — an inconsistency from a threshold that happens to fall between the two weapon speeds.
gaps.evidence: bots.js:570 — if (def.speed && def.speed < 600 && seen && t.vel) lead = dist / def.speed. The AR is speed 300 so it leads; the sniper is speed 700 so it does not (royale.js:55, 63). At the sniper's 90m preferred range that is 0.13s of flight, and against a target sprinting at MOVE.sprint 9.6 m/s that is ~1.2m of un-led error — more than the 0.45m capsule radius. Sniper bots therefore systematically miss anyone moving, at every tier.
gaps.recommendation: Raise the threshold to < 900 so both projectile weapons lead (the hitscan 999-speed guns still correctly skip it), or scale the lead fraction by tier so low-tier bots under-lead deliberately. One-character fix for the first version.

gaps.gap: Two of the six personalities are close to cosmetic, so the behavioural variety is thinner than the personality list implies.
gaps.evidence: Grepping the personality string across bots.js: 'rusher' appears in 4 decisions, 'sniper' and 'camper' gate CAMP and its radius, 'flanker' controls strafe persistence and lateral magnitude, 'loot_goblin' does exactly two things (far-POI drop at bots.js:86, +25 LOOT at bots.js:166), and 'rotator' does exactly two (counts as a hot dropper at bots.js:82, eligible for PUSH at bots.js:182). Nothing in the file makes a 'rotator' rotate earlier or hold zone edges, which is what the name promises. Across a 49-bot lobby the observable variety is roughly three archetypes, not six.
gaps.recommendation: Give each personality one signature decision it alone makes: rotator = rotScore thresholds scaled ~1.4x so it leaves visibly early and takes zone edges; loot_goblin = seeks chests specifically (weight chest score up ~1.5x) and prefers to third-party after a fight rather than initiate; camper = holds a spot and only fires inside ~45m rather than plinking. Personalities are the cheapest source of perceived variety and half the budget here is currently unspent.

gaps.gap: Zero behavioural test coverage for the system that IS the game — the selftest only checks arithmetic on the tier tables.
gaps.evidence: royale.selftest.cjs:150-154 asserts the tier mixes sum to 49, the name pool is >= 60, and that BOT_TIERS[4].aimErrDeg < BOT_TIERS[0].aimErrDeg. Nothing asserts anything about behaviour, because bots.js imports three.js, weapons.js and player.js and cannot run under node. There is no test that bots kill each other, that the alive count decays plausibly, that no bot ends a match stuck, or that a bot ever ends a match with an upgraded weapon — and the file's own comment history (bots.js:359-366 on stuck detection that could never fire, bots.js:471-477 on ensureGunOut being dead code for every bot in every match) shows exactly this class of silent multi-match regression happening twice already.
gaps.recommendation: Extract the decision layer — think(), perceive(), pickLoot(), slotScore(), ensureGunOut(), arcPitch() — behind the same pure-module pattern sim/royale.js already uses, so it can be exercised from node against a stub world. Then add regression assertions on outcomes rather than internals: over a fast-forwarded headless match, at least N bot-on-bot kills occur, fewer than M bots are stuck at the end, and the median bot has traded up off the starter pistol by T seconds. Given the multiplayer cap of 8 humans (net.js:5), bot quality is not a feature of this game — it is the game — and it is currently the only major system with no outcome test.

verdict: Last Circle has a real, working, well-surfaced progression layer inside the match — a persistent XP/level bar, three live challenge cards, a level-up banner that names its reward, and a lifetime career line on the menu — which is more than most browser 3D shooters ship at all. What it does not have is anything that operates on a timescale longer than one match: no daily reset, no leaderboard, no cloud save, and a reward table that runs dry at level 10 after roughly 4-6 hours, at which point every level-up announces "RANK UP" and pays nothing.
what_last_circle_does: Persistent level/XP + lifetime career in localStorage key `lc_progress` (hud.js:1134-1177, loadProgress/saveProgress/recordMatch). Curve: `xpForLevel(l) = 800 + (l-1)*700` (hud.js:1174) — L1→2 = 800 XP, L9→10 = 6,400 XP, cumulative to L10 = 32,400 XP. Match XP (hud.js:2240): `kills*100 + damage*0.2 + (50 - placement)*6 + 500 if victory + timeS/4`. Three per-match challenges drawn from a 5-entry pool (hud.js:1185-1197); slots 0 and 1 are ALWAYS "Survive 3 minutes" (150 XP) and "Get 1 elimination" (175 XP), the third rotates by `level % 3` among "Deal 300 damage" (140), "Reach the final 10" (200), "Get 3 eliminations" (300). All three are evaluated independently each frame and gated on `W.player.alive`, so a spectating corpse cannot bank them. Rewards: 5 character skins at unlock levels 1, 1, 3, 6, 10 (hud.js MENU_SKINS, ends at hud.js:124) — three earnable items total, nothing above level 10 (`levelUpSub` falls through to the string "RANK UP"). Career fields tracked: matches, wins, kills, damage, bestPlacement, top10s, timeAliveS (hud.js:1134); displayed: matches/wins/kills/best on the menu strip and matches/wins/kills/top10s/best on the post-match card — `damage` and `timeAliveS` are accumulated (hud.js:1158-1159) and rendered nowhere. Practice mode is excluded from both XP and career (the sandbox has an unlimited-damage dummy). Match length from royale.js STORM_PHASES: standard = 80+80, 60+70, 50+60, 45+50, 40+45, 30+40, 25+35, 20+45 = 775s (12:55); quick = 239s (~4:00). A worked average standard match (die #20, 1 kill, 250 damage, 5:00 alive) pays 405 match XP + 325 challenge XP = ~730; a strong match ~1,300-1,600; so the full 32,400 XP to level 10 is ~25-45 matches, ~4-6 hours, after which progression pays nothing forever. No daily reset, no streak, no leaderboard, no achievements, no cloud save, no account, no season track, and no UI anywhere to set `playerName` (it exists in the settings defaults at ffg_royale3d.js:420 but no field renders it — offline you are "You" in your own kill feed, online you become "Player-XYZ", net.js:117).
what_benchmarks_do: Final Drop's own progression specifics could NOT be verified — the CrazyGames listing (rated 9.2/10, released June 2026, updated 17 June 2026) and final-drop.com return no XP/level/challenge/season detail, and I found no wiki or review that documents them. The repo's own AUDIT_16LENS.md:47 and :424 assert Final Drop keys its meta off a daily reset and rotates challenges from pools of dozens; that is the team's secondhand observation and I could not confirm it. VERIFIED same-medium bar instead — ZombsRoyale.io (100-player browser BR, the canonical peer): 100-tier battle pass, seasons lasting a few weeks with season-exclusive cosmetics, 1,000 XP per season level = 5 stars, 10 stars per tier, 3 daily challenges every 24 hours (1 hard + 2 normal = 20 stars), and 6 sets of 7 weekly challenges (5 stars normal / 10 hard, 50 stars per set), plus leaderboards ranking eliminations-per-match and time-survived. VERIFIED platform bar — CrazyGames requires cross-device progress sync: "Players care A LOT about their progress in games, and expect their progress to synchronize across their devices", implemented via the Data module, a custom backend, or automatic progress save; games must implement at least one unless progress is not applicable. VERIFIED medium benchmarks (GameAnalytics 2024) — median session 5-6 minutes, top-quartile 8-9 minutes, ~4 sessions/day; median D7 retention 3.4-3.9%, top quartile 7-8%. AAA (Fortnite, loosely verified): 100-tier pass, 85 cosmetic rewards + 800 V-Bucks, season under 60 days, daily + weekly quests; the transferable part for a browser game is the daily reset and the long tiered free track, not the paid pass.
